cards.text: The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, just asked who knows what is good for a man in his few, fleeting days that pass like a shadow (Eccl 1:1; 6:12). Now he answers with a string of things that are better than other things. First up: a good name is better than fine perfume.

cards.question: Right after the perfume line, the Teacher compares two days in a person's life. True or false: he says a person's day of birth is better than his day of death.

cards.text: Then he says it's better to enter a house of mourning than a house of feasting. Friend, the man is walking PAST the party to get to the house where everybody's crying, and he's doing it ON PURPOSE.

cards.question: Why does the Teacher say the house of mourning is the better place to go?

cards.text: Next he says sorrow is better than laughter, for a sad countenance is good for the heart. Friend, after all those years of sad face in the back of a junk drawer, my heart should be running MARATHONS.

cards.question: The Teacher sorts out where people's hearts are. True or false: he says the heart of the wise is in the house of pleasure.

cards.text: Then he puts two sounds side by side: a wise man's rebuke and the song of fools. One of those is a catchy tune, and the other one is your boss saying, “Got a minute? Close the door.”

cards.question: The Teacher says it is better to ___ a wise man's rebuke than to listen to the song of fools.
The Teacher says the laughter of the fool is like a certain sound. Which sound?

answers.text: The crackling of thorns under the pot
The clanging of a cymbal in the street
The rumbling of chariot wheels at the gate

cards.text: Pop, pop, CRACKLE. I bet that racket under the pot doesn't last long, and the Teacher's verdict on it: “This too is futile.”
Back to the Teacher's list, and now a warning about what can wreck even a wise man. He says extortion turns a wise man into a fool.

cards.question: In the same verse as his warning about extortion, the Teacher says a bribe corrupts the heart. True or false?

cards.text: Then he says the end of a matter is better than the beginning. Friend, the beginning of a batch is flour in my mustache and dough on the ceiling, but the end is a sealed cookie box and me GLOWING.

cards.question: In that same line about endings and beginnings, the Teacher compares two kinds of spirit. Which one does he call better?
The Teacher says not to be quickly provoked in your spirit, for anger settles in the lap of a ___.

cards.text: Then he heads off a question people love to ask: “Why were the old days better than these?” Friend, I asked that EVERY night in the junk drawer, and now look at me with a whole PLANET.

cards.question: True or false: the Teacher says it is wise to ask why the old days were better than these.

cards.text: Then he praises wisdom. He says it's good, like an inheritance, and it benefits those who see the sun.

cards.question: The Teacher says wisdom, like money, is a shelter. What advantage of wisdom does he point to?

answers.text: It preserves the life of its owner
It brings its owner great honor
It wins its owner many friends

cards.text: Then the Teacher says to consider the work of God. And he asks a question about what God has bent.

cards.question: The Teacher asks who can ___ what God has bent.

cards.text: Last, he talks about two kinds of days: the day of prosperity and the day of adversity. Payday or flat tire, the man has a word for each one.

cards.question: What does the Teacher say to do in the day of prosperity?
In the day of adversity, the Teacher says to consider something. True or false: God has made the day of adversity along with the day of prosperity.
Why does the Teacher say God made the day of prosperity and the day of adversity together?

answers.text: So a man cannot discover what comes after him
So people learn to save up for hard times
So the proud are humbled and brought down low
